analysis.one_liner: Makes plastic producers pay to collect and recycle their packaging and bans many single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 94 cosponsors—all Democrats—but never got a hearing or a vote in any of its four committees before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shift the cost of dealing with plastic waste from taxpayers and local governments to the companies that make and sell packaged products. It would require producers to fund collection, recycling, and composting of their packaging; set national recycling targets; create a 10-cent deposit refund on beverage containers nationwide; ban single-use plastic bags, plastic utensils, and other throwaway plastic items; temporarily block new or expanded plastic-manufacturing permits until pollution rules are updated; and restrict exporting plastic waste to other countries. It died in committee without any hearings or votes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people get a cleaner environment: fewer single-use plastics, a nationwide 10-cent refund for returning bottles and cans, standardized recycling labels, less plastic exported overseas, and a pause on new plastic plants until their pollution rules catch up. People living near plastic manufacturing and waste facilities, and coastal and low-income communities that bear the brunt of plastic pollution, would benefit most. Local and state governments would also save, since producers—not taxpayers—would fund waste management.

how_it_helps.text: Producers of packaging, paper, and single-use products must pay for collecting, managing, and recycling or composting what they sell, ending the practice of leaving those costs to taxpayers and cities [S2] [S3].
Consumers get at least a 10-cent refund on every beverage container they return to a retailer or redemption center, with retailers required to take back containers [S3].
The bill phases out single-use plastic bags, plastic utensils, straws (on request for those who need them), styrofoam food service products, and hotel mini-bottles starting in 2022 [S2] [S3].
A temporary moratorium blocks new or expanded permits for plastics manufacturing facilities until regulations address pollution from them [S2].
Export of plastic waste to other countries is limited, and collected material must be managed to standards similar to U.S. or OECD rules rather than dumped abroad [S2] [S3].
Products must carry honest labels—a non-recyclable item can no longer display the chasing-arrows recycling symbol—and national standards for recycling bin labels must be published [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Plastic and packaging manufacturers, beverage companies, and other packaged-goods producers would pay fees to producer-run organizations covering collection, recycling, composting, litter cleanup, and marine cleanup, plus civil penalties up to roughly $70,000 per day for violations. Retailers and restaurants would have to charge and refund deposits and comply with bans on bags and utensils. Some of these costs would likely be passed on to shoppers through prices and deposits.

drawbacks.text: Producer fees and deposit requirements would raise costs for food, beverage, and packaged-goods companies, and some of that would show up in prices paid by consumers, including lower-income households [S3].

Every retailer would have to collect and refund beverage container deposits and refuse plastic bags and utensils, adding compliance burdens, though the bill exempts companies with under $1 million in annual revenue and shields small businesses from repeated fines [S3].

The bill gives the EPA administrator broad discretion to define recyclability, ban additional products, and adjust targets by regulation, which critics would call an outsized delegation of power to one agency [S3].

Producers would run the recycling system themselves through industry-created 'Producer Responsibility Organizations,' and the bill exempts those organizations' plan-implementation conduct from antitrust laws—a structure critics note lets the same companies that made the waste control the cleanup system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit—less plastic pollution, cleaner waterways, refunds on containers, and shifting waste costs off taxpayers—is large and durable. The main costs are higher prices and compliance burdens concentrated on producers, retailers, and restaurants, with small businesses partially shielded. The design has a real tension: it charges industry for cleanup but hands industry the machinery of the cleanup system, so its success would depend on aggressive EPA oversight of the producer organizations and their fee structures.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four committees in February 2020, none of them ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Lowenthal introduced the bill on February 11, 2020, joined by 29 original cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S5].
It was referred to four committees—Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Foreign Affairs—meaning any of them could have taken it up [S5].
A day later it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee of Transportation and Infrastructure; that was the last recorded action [S5].
Over the remaining ten-plus months of the Congress, no committee held a markup, no hearing record appears, and the bill never received a floor vote in the House or Senate [S1] [S5].
By the end, 94 House members had cosponsored it, all of them Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastic and packaging manufacturers and beverage companies were better off because the bill died: they avoided producer fees, a national 10-cent deposit program, recycled-content mandates, the permit moratorium on new plastic plants, and bans on their single-use products. State and local governments and taxpayers also kept paying the waste-management costs the bill would have shifted to producers.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 197 House Republicans signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill puts a temporary moratorium on new or expanded plastics plant permits until pollution rules catch up, mandates recycled content in plastic bottles, and helps phase out single-use plastic products—cutting into a growth market for virgin plastic. Its defeat left the industry free to keep expanding.

They would fund collection, recycling, composting, and litter cleanup for every container and package they sell, run a 10-cent national deposit program, and face daily penalties for noncompliance. Because the bill died, those externalized waste costs stayed on taxpayers and cities.

industries.industry: Waste hauling, recycling, and composting industry
industries.note: The bill would have routed producer fees through new producer-run organizations that must spend at least half their money building U.S. recycling and composting infrastructure and pay waste handlers full cost for collection—a large, permanent new funding stream for the recycling sector.

Retailers would have to charge and refund container deposits, accept returned bottles, and drop plastic bags and utensils, though companies under $1 million in revenue get exemptions and fine caps. Compliance costs would fall mainly on larger chains.
